lessons.title: What a viability test is and preparing for it
lessons.html:
What a viability test is and preparing for it

A germination test takes days or weeks. Sometimes a seed company needs a quick answer: is this seed alive? The viability test, usually the tetrazolium (TZ) test, answers that in one or two days. Living tissue in the seed turns the colourless tetrazolium solution into a red stain. Dead tissue stays white. By looking at which parts of the embryo are stained, the analyst estimates how many seeds are able to germinate.

The TZ test is useful for dormant seed, for a quick check before buying a lot from a seed grower, and to explain why a germination test gave a poor result. It does not replace the germination test on the label.

Prepare the work area

  • Clean the bench and tools: scalpels or razor blades, forceps, needles, petri dishes, beakers and a magnifier or stereo microscope.
  • Check that the incubator or oven used for staining is at the temperature in your procedure.
  • Prepare or check the tetrazolium solution as your laboratory procedure states. It must be fresh and kept in a dark bottle, because light breaks it down.
  • Label containers with the sample number before you start.

Safety

Tetrazolium salt and some treated seeds are hazardous. Wear gloves and a lab coat, use eye protection when preparing solutions, and read the safety data sheet. Sharp blades cause many lab injuries: cut away from your fingers, use a holder and dispose of used blades in a sharps container. Never eat or drink in the laboratory.

Documentation

Open a worksheet with the sample number, crop, lot, number of seeds and replicates, the preconditioning method, staining time and temperature, and your name. The testing rules your laboratory follows (usually ISTA rules) set the method for each crop.

lessons.title: Imbibition and preparing seed for staining
lessons.html:
Imbibition and preparing seed for staining

Dry seed does not stain well. The seeds must first take up water, which is called imbibition or preconditioning. Water softens the seed, starts the living processes and makes cutting easier.

Prepare the working sample for imbibition

  1. Take the working sample from pure seed, mixed well.
  2. Count out the replicates at random. Do not choose the best-looking seeds.
  3. Place seeds between moist paper or soak them in water, as the method for the crop requires. Some seeds, such as large legumes, are better slowly moistened on paper so they do not crack.
  4. Leave them for the time and temperature in the method, often overnight.
  5. Record start and end times.

Preparing seeds for staining

The stain must reach the embryo. Depending on the crop, the analyst:

  • Cuts the seed lengthwise through the embryo, for example maize and other cereals, so that half the embryo is exposed.
  • Pierces or cuts off a small piece of the seed away from the embryo.
  • Removes the seed coat for some legumes and other seeds.

Cut cleanly and carefully. Crushing or tearing the embryo damages it and makes it look dead when it is not. Keep prepared seeds moist while you work so they do not dry out.

Staining

  1. Place the prepared seeds in the labelled dish and cover them completely with tetrazolium solution.
  2. Keep the dishes in the dark, in the incubator, for the time set in the method.
  3. Do not over-stain. Seeds left too long become very dark and are hard to read.
  4. Pour off the solution and rinse the seeds with water when staining time is complete.

Dispose of used solution as your laboratory waste procedure requires, never down a drain that leads to a stream or dam.

lessons.title: Evaluating the stained seed and completing the test
lessons.html:
Evaluating the stained seed and completing the test

Evaluation is a skilled task. You look at each seed under the magnifier and decide whether it is viable based on where the red stain appears and how it looks.

Reading the staining pattern

AppearanceUsual meaning
Even, bright red stain over the whole embryoViable, healthy tissue
Unstained (white) areas in critical parts, such as the root tip or the point where root and shoot joinNon-viable
Very dark red or purple, mottled tissueDamaged or deteriorating tissue
No stain at allDead seed

Small unstained areas in non-critical parts may still allow a normal seedling. The handbook for the crop shows which areas are critical. When you are unsure, ask a senior analyst and compare with reference photos.

Counting and calculating

  1. Sort each seed of each replicate into viable or non-viable.
  2. Count each replicate separately and record the numbers.
  3. Calculate the percentage viable for each replicate and the average.
  4. Check that replicates agree within the tolerance in the testing rules. If not, repeat the test.

Completing the process

  • Complete the worksheet: counts, percentage viable, observations such as insect damage or mechanical cracks, and your signature.
  • Pass the result on for checking and reporting.
  • Dispose of stained seeds and solution according to the waste procedure.
  • Clean and disinfect dishes, blades and the bench. Put blades in the sharps container.
  • Return the unused tetrazolium solution to dark, cool storage if it may be kept, or discard it.

A big difference between viability and germination results can show dormancy (viable but not germinating) or problems with the germination test itself. Note this on the report so the manager can follow up.

Key points

  • The tetrazolium test shows living tissue as red stain and gives a quick answer.
  • Seeds must be imbibed before cutting and staining.
  • Cut cleanly; damaged embryos look dead.
  • Unstained critical areas mean the seed is non-viable.
  • Wear gloves, handle blades safely and dispose of solution correctly.
